```{python}
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

# DATA 202 hack for displaying plotly within RStudio:
if 'r' in globals() and r['.Platform$GUI'] == "RStudio" and r['suppressMessages(requireNamespace("htmltools"))']:
  r[".GlobalEnv$to_html <- function(x) { print(htmltools::HTML(x)) }"] and None
  def show_plot(p): r.to_html(p._repr_html_())
else:
  def show_plot(p): return p
# End hack
```

::: {.callout-important}
Please shutdown your RStudio session when you're not using it.
:::

## Data

```{python}
#| echo: true
gapminder = px.data.gapminder()
gapminder_latest = gapminder.query("year == 2007")
just_usa = gapminder.query("country == 'United States'")

countries = [
  "China", "India", "United States",
  "Indonesia", "Brazil", "Pakistan",
  "Bangladesh", "Nigeria", "Japan"]

gapminder_9_countries = gapminder.query("country in @countries")
```


## Univariate analysis - Continuous

Pick one of the continuous variables. Make two different types of plots to show its distribution.  (Use `gapminder_latest`, which has one row per country.)

```{python}
px.histogram(gapminder_latest, x = "lifeExp")
```

```{python}
px.violin(gapminder_latest, x = "lifeExp")
```

```{python}
px.box(gapminder_latest, x = "lifeExp")
```

## Univariate Analysis - Categorical

Make a bar plot of the number of countries by continent. (Use `gapminder_latest`, which has one row per country.)

```{python}
px.histogram(gapminder_latest, x = "continent")
```

Discuss the interpretation of this plot with your partner. (Why is this a `histogram` and not a `bar` plot?)

Try adjusting the plot to make the countries easier to read.


## Bivariate: Relationship between numerical and categorical

Pick one of the continuous variables and plot its relationship with `continent`.

Note:

- You may again want to use only 2007 data (`gapminder_latest`)
- You may want to try using `log(variable)` instead of `variable`.

Make two different visualizations. Compare and contrast them.

```{python}
px.box(gapminder_latest, x = "lifeExp", y = "continent")
```

```{python}
px.violin(gapminder_latest, x = "lifeExp", y = "continent")
```

## Bivariate with a discrete variable

Try plotting how the *distribution* of one of the continuous variables changes by `year`.
Try making two different distribution plots.
At least one of them should be a ridge plot.
What do you notice about what has happened to the *shape* of the different variables over the years?

::: {.callout-tip}
You might need to set `orientation = "h"` to tell plotly which variable is the discrete one (since both have a numeric storage type).
:::


```{python}
px.box(gapminder, x = "year", y = "lifeExp")
```

```{python}
px.box(gapminder, y = "year", x = "lifeExp", orientation = "h")
```

```{python}
(
    px.violin(gapminder, y = "year", x = "lifeExp", orientation = "h")
    .update_traces(side = "positive", width=15)
)
```

```{python}
(
    px.violin(gapminder, y = "year", x = "gdpPercap", orientation = "h")
    .update_traces(side = "positive", width=15)
)
```
